prompt: Write a ~700-word piece of literary short fiction about: a bricklayer building his last wall. Prose only, no headings.
text:
As he stepped out into the morning's pale light, the bricklayer took stock of the job ahead. Not much left to do now – just this one wall, capping off a career spent laying courses and stacks, mortars and pointing. Thirty years, give or take, and it was coming down to this: his last wall.

He stretched, feeling the familiar ache in his lower back, and reached for his trowel, already lying where he'd left it on the scaffold. The tools had been cleaned and put away after each day's work for months now – a habit that seemed to be hardwiring itself into his very being. He liked order; a well-run site was a happy one.

A light breeze rustled the weeds sprouting from cracks in the old pavement, sending faint whispers through the air. The bricklayer breathed it in, feeling a sense of nostalgia creep over him. It started as soon as he'd accepted this would be his last project – memories flooding back, like autumn's colours bursting across the trees. His grandfather, teaching him how to mix mortar when he was just a boy; the satisfying click of a new brick settling into place for the first time; the countless nights spent watching the stars, lying on his own makeshift scaffold as a young man.

He shook himself free from the reverie and began measuring out the materials. A standard height, with maybe an extra course to cap it off. Not too fiddly – no need to get anxious about this one. As he worked, laying each brick into place with practiced ease, a sense of calm washed over him. This was what he'd done best in his life: building walls that stood strong and true.

His mind kept drifting back to the memories, though – the faces of apprentices he'd trained, now running their own sites; the countless clients who'd thanked him for creating spaces that felt like a part of themselves. He remembered one particularly tricky job on a cold winter's morning, when a young couple had turned up at 6 am with a newborn baby in tow. They'd wanted a quiet space for feeding and changing diapers, and he'd promised to get it done by the end of the day. The satisfaction he felt as they watched their little one sleep peacefully amidst the tidy rows of brickwork...

A brick slipped from his hand, landing with a faint thud against the scaffold's metal frame. He picked it up, dusting off the mortar that had started to set – more than enough time for him to correct the mistake before anyone would notice. As he re-laid the brick, his thoughts turned to his own children; how proud they'd been of their dad when he was working on a new site, taking them along to watch the progress.

He finished the row and stepped back to admire it – a few minor adjustments still needed, but that could wait till tomorrow. Not much longer now. His mind wandered to the thought of retirement: what would he do with himself? There were plans for travel, maybe even learning new skills in his spare time... or perhaps just drifting aimlessly through days filled with nothing but the gentle hum of silence.

For a moment, as the sun climbed higher and cast its warm light across the brickwork, he allowed himself to imagine an empty life – no deadlines, no clients breathing down his neck. A blank slate, waiting for whatever came next. But even as this notion took hold, another memory burst forth: the day he'd first hung up his shingle, a young man with big dreams and an even bigger ego.

The wall was almost complete now. He'd make one more pass around it tomorrow – maybe add some finishing touches – but essentially, that would be it. His last brick would go into place, marking the end of a chapter. It felt strange to think about leaving this life behind; he'd spent so long defining himself by his work.

The afternoon sun crept over the rooftops as he began packing up his tools and giving the site one final tidy. This was it: thirty years of bricklaying coming down to this – one last wall, standing proud in a quiet corner of the city, waiting for whatever future lay beyond its neat rows.
topic: a bricklayer building his last wall
